comments.name: Arun Adhikari
comments.text:
This paper is bigger than just “US vs China.”
What we’re really witnessing is the beginning of an AI-powered geopolitical era where intelligence infrastructure may become as important as oil, nuclear technology, or the internet itself. 🌍🤖

The country that leads in frontier AI could influence: • global economics,
• cyber security,
• military systems,
• scientific discovery,
• education,
• and even cultural narratives worldwide.

What makes this race different from previous technology races is the speed. AI models are improving exponentially while governments, laws, and international institutions are moving much slower.

But the most important question is not simply: “Who wins the AI race?”

It’s: What happens to the rest of the world if only a few nations control superintelligence-level systems?

Smaller countries could become digitally dependent the same way many became economically dependent during previous industrial revolutions.

This is why open research, global cooperation, and ethical governance matter just as much as raw technological power. Because the future of AI should not become a monopoly of either corporations or governments.

The next world superpower may not be defined by land, population, or weapons alone but by compute, data, energy, and AI capability. 🚀

comments.name: Pierre
comments.text:
As a French, I think you are on the wrong path there, lecturing the world with your supremacist vision about democracy. This is very old school thinking, 20th century post WW2 but no longer applicable today...

You are conflating democracy with technological progress, which does not really make sense !

The irony is that your own model is not open source, while many Chinese companies and researchers, from a country you describe as “non-democratic” which seems to be a central point in your argument, are actually contributing more to the open source AI ecosystem.

I also find it striking how many keynote presentations portray your llm as some kind of flawless revolution, with speakers appearing almost mesmerized by their own narrative, as if there were no serious limitations or risks ahead. One major blind spot seems to be the enormous infrastructure and power-grid requirements needed to sustain these models at scale.
We are constantly shown promotional videos claiming that, with the “right prompt” and the proper orchestration of skills or agents, users can magically unlock the full potential of the model. But perhaps that is precisely the issue: the systems themselves are difficult to calibrate consistently because compute capacity remains constrained. As a result, users are asked to manually activate certain capabilities, disable others, and constantly fine-tune workflows, instead of interacting with something that functions robustly and autonomously on its own.

Another is privacy: in order to benefit from your most advanced capabilities, users’ data still has to transit through and be processed on your servers. We are told that paid versions are “not used for training” but that does not entirely address the underlying concern, since the provider still potentially has access to highly sensitive or private information.
This is precisely where open-source and locally deployable models have a strong advantage (unfortunately still costly for an entrepreneur to deploy at home): they can reduce dependency on centralized infrastructures and allow users or companies to keep sensitive data within their own controlled environments.
